result:
The cache in `final.py` scores **0.5621** on the search split, against **0.365** for the LRU baseline. I used **19 of the 24 scorer calls** and about 9 of the 15-minute budget I set at the start. I stopped early because the last five variants all came out flat or worse on my local test harness. I couldn't run a held-out check through the scorer, because this `./score` only covers the search split. The held-out numbers below come from my own generated traces, using seeds I never tuned on.

| | search (scorer) | held-out (my harness) |
|---|---|---|
| Baseline (LRU) | 0.365 | 0.302 |
| First champion (W-TinyLFU) | 0.522 | 0.335 |
| **Final pick** | **0.562** | **0.423** |

On the scorer's six traces, the final pick gets: hot_with_scans 0.249, loop_and_hot 0.660, phases 0.637, mixed 0.267, recency 0.847, shifting_loops 0.712. A full scoring run takes about 2 seconds, well inside the 8-second limit.

**Why it beats LRU:** it is a W-TinyLFU cache: a new key only displaces an older one if it has been requested more often recently. That keeps hot keys in the cache through scans, and keeps a fixed part of a loop cached instead of losing all of it. The catch is that no single setting suits every pattern:
- Recency-heavy traffic wants a large recency window (close to LRU).
- Loops want no window at all (purely frequency-based).
- Shifting popularity wants request counts to fade quickly; steady patterns want them to fade slowly.

So `final.py` runs 20 small simulated caches alongside the real one: 5 window sizes (0, 1, 20, 50 and 95% of capacity) × 4 fading speeds. Each tracks its own recent hit rate, and on every request the real cache takes the settings of whichever is currently doing best. It never needs to add anything other than the requested key. This matched ARC on recency (0.847) and kept TinyLFU's loop performance, and the extra fading speeds lifted shifting_loops from 0.65 to 0.71.

**Approaches tried at first (scorer score):**
- LRU: 0.365
- ARC: 0.407 (strong on recency, collapses on loops)
- S3-FIFO: harness only, between ARC and TinyLFU
- W-TinyLFU: 0.522
- W-TinyLFU with a hill-climbing window size (Caffeine-style): 0.536

Ideas tested only on the harness, with no gain: continuous count decay (it broke loop protection), counter ceilings of 7 or 63, ties admitting the new key, a hysteresis margin before switching, simulating the side caches on a 1/4 sample of keys, duelling over the protected-segment share, and picking the eviction victim as the least-used of the 4 oldest.

**What worked:** letting a scored choice between fixed settings decide, rather than a hill climber, whose random drift cost hits on loops. Duelling over how fast counts fade gave the second big jump. My harness overweighted recency, so I relied on scorer calls to judge loop behaviour.

All candidates and harness scripts (`harness2.py`, `sweep.py`, `opt.py`) are in the folder next to `final.py`.

Two connected services, Atlassian Rovo and HyperFrames by HeyGen, need authorizing in your claude.ai connector settings before they can be used. This task didn't need them.
